lessons.title: Common Mistakes: Chasing Peak Cyclicals, Overpaying for Safety, and Timing the Turn

body.text: Almost every expensive mistake in this course comes from one of three habits: trusting a number that is measured at the wrong point in the cycle, trusting a label instead of the holdings, or acting after the evidence is already public and priced in.

children.text: This lesson collects the errors the earlier chapters exposed, with the evidence attached. None of them are exotic. They are the ordinary, reasonable-sounding decisions that cost Indian investors money in every cycle, and most of them can be avoided with a single check before you buy.

children.text: This one is dangerous because every signal points the same way at once. Profits are at records, margins are at decade highs, the P/E is in single digits, return on equity looks superb, the dividend has been raised, and the company is announcing an expansion. Each fact is true. Together they describe the top of a cycle, because peak earnings shrink the P/E and inflate ROE at the same moment.

body.title: The Arithmetic of the Trap
body.prompt: You buy a metal stock at 5 times its peak EPS of ₹50, so you pay ₹250. Two years later earnings normalise to ₹20, and the market now values it at 10 times those normalised earnings. What is your return, in percent? Enter a negative number if you lost money.
body.explanation: New price = 10 × ₹20 = ₹200, against ₹250 paid, a loss of 20%. Note what happened: the P/E doubled from 5 to 10, which looks like the market getting more optimistic, and you still lost money because earnings fell 60%. This is why Chapter 4 insisted on normalised earnings.

body.text: The tell for peak cyclicality is agreement. When the low P/E, the record margin, the high ROE, the dividend increase, and the capex announcement all arrive in the same quarter, treat it as a warning rather than confirmation. Check the operating margin against its 10-year range first; if it is near the top, the cheap-looking P/E is measuring peak earnings.

children.text: The mirror image. Here the business really is excellent, the earnings really are stable, and the mistake is entirely in the price. Chapter 3 showed the arithmetic: buy at 60 times earnings, watch EPS grow 10% a year for four years, and if the multiple settles at 40, your share price is slightly lower than where you started. Chapter 4 showed it happening in the market, where Asian Paints delivered 37.8% EPS growth from its January 2022 peak to July 2026 while the share price fell 23.2%.

stats.label: Its P/E over the same period

children.text: Mistake 3: Trying to Time the Turn

Timing fails in both directions, and for opposite reasons. Investors who wait for proof buy late: in 2020, the Nifty 50 bottomed on 23 March, while zero car sales, a PMI of 27.4, and a 55.5% fall in industrial production were published between 39 and 81 days afterwards. Investors who act on conviction alone buy early and often sell before the recovery arrives, which is what the Chapter 3 switcher did, selling metals near the bottom and buying them back after the rally.

body.title: Two Ways to Get the Turn Wrong

columns.label: Waiting for certainty
points: Requires improving earnings before buying a cyclical
By then the stock has usually rerated
Feels responsible, costs the best part of the recovery
Fix: act on valuation and direction of change, not on confirmation

columns.label: Switching on emotion
points: Sells cyclicals after a crash and buys them after a rally
Follows recent performance in both directions
Feels like decisive action, locks in the worst of both
Fix: a written target mix and a rebalancing rule

body.title: Spot the Real Warning
body.question: A cement company reports its best-ever operating margin, its P/E has fallen to 8, ROE is at a decade high, and it has just announced a 40% capacity expansion funded partly by debt. What is the most useful interpretation?
options: A cheap, high-quality compounder worth buying aggressively
Several signs that earnings are at or near a cyclical peak, which makes the low P/E misleading
Nothing can be concluded without the dividend yield
The debt-funded expansion guarantees higher future profits
body.explanation: Record margins compress the P/E and inflate ROE simultaneously. Industry-wide expansion at the top of a cycle is what creates the next oversupply, and debt raises financial leverage into the downturn. The right next step is to calculate the P/E on mid-cycle margins, as Chapter 4 showed.

children.text: A consumption index with about 36% in autos and consumer durables is not a defensive holding, and a low volatility index selects on price calm rather than earnings stability.
Five stocks across five sectors can still be five ways to own the same economic cycle, especially if your salary depends on it too.
Reading a ratio without its context.

A ROCE collapse can mean an acquisition rather than a weakening business, as HUL showed after the GSK Consumer Healthcare merger, and a coefficient of variation above 0.3 can simply mean the company grew steadily.
Telecom behaved like a deep cyclical during the price war and more like a defensive after consolidation. Re-check at least once a year.

body.label: Three questions before any cyclical or defensive decision
body.value: Where in the cycle is this earnings number? What does the price already assume? What else in my life depends on the same cycle?
body.context: If you cannot answer all three, you are not ready to act

body.title: Diagnose the Portfolio
body.scenario: Prakash, 41, works for a commercial vehicle maker. His equity portfolio: 25% in a steel company bought last quarter at a P/E of 6 after record results, 20% in a capital goods stock bought after two strong years, 15% in his employer's shares, 20% in an IT sector fund bought at the start of 2022, and 20% in a consumption fund he considers his defensive allocation. He says he is diversified across five holdings and two sectors he understands well.
body.prompt: List the mistakes from this lesson that appear in Prakash's portfolio, and what you would do first.
body.modelAnswer: At least five. First, chasing a peak cyclical: buying steel at a P/E of 6 right after record results is the low P/E trap, since that multiple is measured on peak earnings. Second, buying last year's winner: the capital goods position came after two strong years, and the IT fund was bought at the start of 2022, just before Nifty IT fell 26.0%. Third, trusting a label: the consumption fund is roughly 36% autos and consumer durables, so his defensive allocation is substantially cyclical. Fourth, counting names instead of cycles: steel, capital goods, employer stock, and much of the consumption fund all depend on the same industrial cycle. Fifth, ignoring human capital: his salary and employer shares add a sixth and seventh exposure to commercial vehicles. What to do first is not to sell everything, which would just be another emotional switch. Start by measuring: classify every holding, add up the true cyclical share including his employer stock, and compare it with a target mix chosen from horizon, income cyclicality, and drawdown tolerance. Then close the gap using fresh investments into genuine defensives and diversified funds, cap employer stock as a share of net worth, and build an emergency fund so a downturn in his industry never forces him to sell at the bottom.

body.title: The Core Confusion
body.textWithBlank: Most of these mistakes trace back to reading a company's ___ instead of its earnings through a full cycle.
body.explanation: Share prices reflect sentiment, flows, and valuation changes as well as business performance. Earnings across a full cycle are what actually tell you whether a company is cyclical or defensive.

cards.definition: Buying a cyclical because its P/E looks cheap, when the low multiple is caused by peak earnings that are about to fall.
Buying a quality defensive at a multiple so high that years of good earnings growth are absorbed by derating.
Waiting for improving data or earnings before buying a cyclical, by which time the stock has usually already rerated.
Assuming a fund or index behaves the way its name suggests, without checking its sector weights and holdings.
Holding many stocks that all depend on the same economic cycle, often alongside an income that depends on it too.

body.title: The Pre-Trade Check
steps: Is this company cyclical or defensive on the evidence of 10 years of earnings, not its share price?
Where does the latest operating margin sit within its 10-year range?
What is the P/E on normalised or mid-cycle earnings, not on the last reported year?
For a defensive, how does the multiple compare with its own long-term median, and how many years of growth would it take to grow into the price?
Has anything structural changed: a new competitor, an acquisition, a regulatory shift?
How much of my portfolio, and my income, already depends on this same cycle?
Am I buying because of the analysis, or because of recent performance?

points: Peak cyclical signals arrive together: low P/E, record margins, high ROE, and industry-wide expansion
A P/E can double while you still lose money, if earnings fall far enough
Overpaying for a genuinely excellent defensive is a valuation mistake, not a business mistake, and it still costs real money
Timing fails both ways: waiting for confirmation buys late, and switching on emotion sells low and buys high
Labels mislead, ratios need context, and classifications expire, so re-check holdings at least once a year
Before acting, ask where the earnings sit in the cycle, what the price already assumes, and what else in your life depends on that cycle
